Spearmen
spēr´měn
n. pl. (troops armed with the spear; the escort that carried Paul out of Jerusalem)
From spear + men. At Acts 23:23 the Greek is dexiolaboi, literally right-hand-takers — a rare military term, probably javelin-men or lictors. At Psalm 68:30 the Hebrew is chayyath qaneh, the beast of the reeds.

Biblical Definition

Forty men have sworn to eat nothing until Paul is dead: “And when it was day, certain of the Jews banded together, and bound themselves under a curse, saying that they would neither eat nor drink till they had killed Paul” (Acts 23:12). The Roman chief captain, learning of it from Paul's nephew, responds with overwhelming force: “And he called unto him two centurions, saying, Make ready two hundred soldiers to go to Caesarea, and horsemen threescore and ten, and spearmen two hundred, at the third hour of the night” (Acts 23:23). Four hundred and seventy men, marched at nine in the evening, to move one prisoner. Luke records the numbers because they are the shape of a promise kept: the night before, “the Lord stood by him, and said, Be of good cheer, Paul: for as thou hast testified of me in Jerusalem, so must thou bear witness also at Rome” (Acts 23:11). God had said Rome, and the Roman army became the means. The Psalmist prays against the same class of power where it is hostile: “Rebuke the company of spearmen, the multitude of the bulls, with the calves of the people, till every one submit himself with pieces of silver: scatter thou the people that delight in war” (Psalm 68:30).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a spearman as one who is armed with a spear; and a spear as a long pointed weapon used in war and hunting.

expand to see more

SPEARMAN, n. One who is armed with a spear.

SPEAR, n. [Sax. spere.] A long, pointed weapon, used in war and hunting, by thrusting or throwing; a lance.

CENTURION, n. [L. centurio, from centum, a hundred.] In the Roman armies, a military officer who commanded a hundred men.

ESCORT, n. [Fr. escorte.] A guard; a body of armed men which attends an officer, or baggage, provisions or munitions, to protect them.

GARRISON, n. A body of troops stationed in a fort or fortified town, to defend it.

Key Scripture

Acts 23:23 — "And he called unto him two centurions, saying, Make ready two hundred soldiers to go to Caesarea, and horsemen threescore and ten, and spearmen two hundred, at the third hour of the night;"

Acts 23:12 — "And when it was day, certain of the Jews banded together, and bound themselves under a curse, saying that they would neither eat nor drink till they had killed Paul."

Acts 23:11 — "And the night following the Lord stood by him, and said, Be of good cheer, Paul: for as thou hast testified of me in Jerusalem, so must thou bear witness also at Rome."

Psalm 68:30 — "Rebuke the company of spearmen, the multitude of the bulls, with the calves of the people, till every one submit himself with pieces of silver: scatter thou the people that delight in war."

Modern Corruption

Providence is expected to arrive by miracle, so that the ordinary machinery God actually uses — a nephew who overhears, an officer who follows procedure — is not recognized as the answer.

expand to see more

Acts 23 is a small masterclass in how God usually keeps His word. The Lord promises Rome on one night; the deliverance the next day comes through a boy who happened to hear something, a centurion who took him seriously, and a garrison commander protecting a Roman citizen because the law required it. Not one of those men was a believer, and not one step of it was miraculous. A Christian waiting for the spectacular can live through an entire answered prayer and file it under coincidence.

The chapter also settles a question about the state. Paul accepts a pagan army's protection without apology, as he had invoked his citizenship at Philippi and would appeal to Caesar later. The magistrate bears the sword for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of them that do well, and a Christian may lawfully use that protection. Psalm 68:30 holds the other half: the same power, turned hostile and delighting in war, is something to pray against. Neither reverence nor contempt for the sword; a doctrine of it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek dexiolabos (G1187), a spearman, right-hand-taker; stratiotes (G4757), a soldier; hekatontarches (G1543), a centurion; Hebrew qaneh (H7070), a reed.

expand to see more

Greek dexiolabos (G1187) — spearman; a rare word, only Acts 23:23.

Greek hekatontarches (G1543) — a centurion; two of them detailed for one prisoner.

Greek anathematizo (G332) — to bind under a curse; the forty men's oath, Acts 23:12.

Hebrew chayyath qaneh (H2416 + H7070) — the beast of the reeds; Psalm 68:30, rendered company of spearmen.

Greek martureo (G3140) — to bear witness; the errand the escort was serving, Acts 23:11.

Usage

"“Spearmen two hundred, at the third hour of the night” — the shape of a promise kept."

"“So must thou bear witness also at Rome” — said the night before."

"“Scatter thou the people that delight in war” — the same power, prayed against."
